title: Forecasting the Next Steps in Ukraine's Military Evolution
gist: RAND's Jacob Parakilas and Oliver Gill argue the Armed Forces of Ukraine face a real institutional fork between a 'Traditionalist' combined-arms/mass-mobilization model and a 'Technologist' model built around the Unmanned Systems Forces, and lay out concrete data (USF is 2% of personnel but drives ~30% of Russian losses) and two detailed scenarios showing neither pure model works alone -- drones and legacy heavy weapons remain mutually dependent.

themes.theme: The two competing theories of victory

insights.claim: Two camps have publicly split within Ukraine's military leadership: a 'Traditionalist' camp associated with recently relieved Chief of General Staff Oleksandr Syrskyi favoring proven combined-arms tactics, and a 'Reformist/Technologist' camp associated with recently dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov favoring decentralized procurement, SMEs, and novel unmanned-systems-led warfare.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Both key figures on either side of this debate were dismissed near-simultaneously, suggesting Ukraine's leadership is groping for a middle path rather than committing fully to either doctrine -- a signal for defense-tech investors betting on either drone-centric or legacy-hardware-centric procurement narratives.
insights.quote: A traditionalist camp, personified by recently relieved Chief of the General Staff Oleksandr Syrskyi... A reformist camp, symbolised by equally recently dismissed Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

insights.claim: The authors argue the Traditionalist-vs-Technologist framing is an oversimplification, since the public rivalry between Syrskyi and Fedorov was as much about political and cultural context and governance philosophy as about military tactics.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Warns analysts against reading Ukraine's military reform debate purely as a tech-adoption story; procurement politics and institutional culture are equally decisive variables.
insights.quote: The distinction between Old and New, static and manoeuvrable, traditional and novel, is perhaps an oversimplification.

themes.theme: The Unmanned Systems Forces: outsized impact, still a minority force

insights.claim: Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) comprise only about 2 percent of the military's personnel strength yet are responsible for roughly 30 percent of Russian losses, while the remaining 98 percent of 'traditional army' personnel account for the other 70 percent of Russian losses.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: A striking productivity ratio (2% of headcount driving 30% of enemy attrition) that quantifies the asymmetric leverage of drone warfare -- a key data point for defense-tech investment theses on unmanned systems' cost-effectiveness versus legacy mass-mobilized infantry.
insights.quote: The USF make up just two percent of the military's personnel strength yet are responsible for roughly 30 percent of Russian losses.
insights.locator: section on the Unmanned Systems Forces

insights.claim: The Unmanned Systems Forces became the world's first branch of a military organized specifically around unmanned systems, codified under General Syrskyi's own tenure -- meaning even the 'traditionalist' figure helped institutionalize the technologist reform.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Undercuts a clean traditionalist/technologist binary -- shows institutional innovation in drone warfare can emerge even under supposedly conservative leadership.
insights.quote: It was under General Syrskyi's tenure that the world's first Unmanned Systems Force was codified as a branch of the armed forces.
insights.locator: section on the Unmanned Systems Forces

insights.claim: The Unmanned Systems Forces make up only 13 of Ukraine's more than 100 total AFU brigades, and all of Ukraine's other force types (land forces, National Guard, territorial defence) also use unmanned systems to varying degrees, blurring the line between 'traditional' and 'novel' units.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Confirms drone adoption is diffusing across the entire force rather than being confined to a specialized branch, implying broader defense-tech procurement demand across all unit types, not just a narrow USF niche.
insights.quote: The distinction between the Unmanned Systems Forces (13 out of over 100 total AFU brigades) on one hand, and the land forces, National Guard, and territorial defence forces on the other, is again not as clear-cut as it may seem.

insights.claim: Under a Traditionalist scenario, Ukraine would continue fielding the maximum number of brigades with fresh recruits evenly distributed across units rather than concentrated in higher-performing formations, preserving broad interoperability with NATO but requiring constant General Staff intervention due to non-contiguous brigade deployment across the frontline.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Describes a scenario prioritizing alliance interoperability at the cost of organizational efficiency -- relevant to assessing how quickly Ukraine could integrate further NATO equipment and doctrine under this path.
insights.quote: As fresh recruits complete basic training, they continue to be more or less evenly distributed across all active units, rather than being preferentially assigned to higher-performing or more combat-effective formations.

insights.claim: Under General Syrskyi, Ukraine's General Basic Military Training was extended from 30 to 51 days, with all soldiers trained first as infantrymen before any potential specialization as uncrewed-systems operators, reflecting persistent risk from Russian infiltration tactics.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable policy data point (30-to-51-day training extension) demonstrating that even under increased automation, foundational infantry skills remain a prioritized institutional investment.
insights.quote: Under General Syrskyi's tenure, General Basic Military Training was extended from 30 to 51 days for standard entry into the Ground Forces.

insights.claim: In the Traditionalist scenario, voluntary recruitment continues to be inadequate for a war of attrition, forcing increasingly coercive mobilization and conscription despite public protest.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Flags rising political/social risk (forced conscription backlash) as a downstream consequence of sticking with a manpower-intensive traditional force structure.
insights.quote: Despite public protest and frustration, more coercive forms of mobilisation and conscription have become necessary to fill the ranks.

insights.claim: The Traditionalist theory of victory holds that only offensive maneuver by assault units -- with unmanned systems in a supporting rather than leading role -- can justly end the war by driving invaders from occupied territory, and warns that over-reliance on autonomous kill-chains risks only prolonging the war.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Articulates the core strategic bet of the Traditionalist camp: decisive territorial reconquest over attritional drone warfare -- a variable that affects expectations for how/when the war could end.
insights.quote: Only by eventually driving the invaders from occupied territory by manoeuvre can the war be ended justly. Offensive action by assault units, with uncrewed systems in a crucial but supporting function, remains indispensable.

insights.claim: Heavy artillery, armoured breachers, and conventional strike assets remain indispensable for reducing hardened, protected infrastructure -- unmanned systems and medium-range strike platforms cannot independently solve every tactical problem.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: A direct counterpoint to pure-drone-warfare narratives -- legacy heavy weapons manufacturers retain a durable demand niche even in a drone-saturated battlefield.
insights.quote: Heavy artillery, armoured breachers, and conventional strike assets have remained indispensable for reducing hardened, protected infrastructure.

insights.claim: In the Technologist scenario, frontline human soldiers shift from direct combat to guarding strongpoints and rear-area logistics/communications, while ISR, defensive fires, short-range strike, and even ground assault are increasingly handled by remote and autonomous systems with humans as a backup force.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Describes a battlefield labor-substitution model (autonomous systems as primary, humans as reserve) directly analogous to automation debates in civilian economies -- relevant to defense-tech investors modeling demand for autonomous ISR/strike platforms.
insights.quote: ISR, defensive fires, short-range strike, and even ground assault are increasingly handled by remote and autonomous systems, with humans serving as a backup force rather than leading the charge.

insights.claim: The Technologist model reduces AFU personnel exposure to enemy direct fire and allows volunteers otherwise unfit for frontline duty to keep contributing, but it also destabilizes existing command structures, increases turnover at higher ranks, and opens seams that Russian forces could exploit both physically and informationally.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Identifies organizational destabilization and exploitable seams as the key downside risk of rapid technologist transformation -- a factor investors in military-AI/robotics should weigh alongside battlefield efficacy claims.
insights.quote: It has also destabilized existing structures, increased turnover at higher ranks, and opened opportunities for Russian forces to exploit seams in Ukrainian defences—both physically and informationally.

insights.claim: Rapid AFU technologist transformation risks outpacing NATO's own force-transformation efforts, creating new obstacles to interoperability between Ukraine and its Western partners.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Flags an alliance-interoperability risk: Ukraine's battlefield-driven innovation could move faster than NATO doctrine/procurement, complicating future joint operations and arms standardization.
insights.quote: The AFU's rapid transformation also risks outpacing NATO's own force-transformation efforts, creating new obstacles to interoperability.

insights.claim: Under the Technologist model, market forces increasingly squeeze out manufacturers previously protected by unregulated contracts, while SMEs seize smaller peripheral contracts and Ukrainian/European drone-primes consolidate market share and scale up, with Ukrainian firms becoming increasingly viable global defense-market players.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Direct signal for investors: Ukraine's drone-manufacturing base is positioned to become a durable export industry and consolidation target as the sector matures, creating tension between domestic wartime needs and export revenue.
insights.quote: Ukrainian firms have become increasingly viable players on the global defence market, but demand for their products has created some tension as the government tries to balance sustainable export success with continuing to feed the needs of the AFU.

insights.claim: The Technologist theory of victory holds that unrestricted technological dominance -- especially medium- and deep-strike capability against Russian logistics and industrial infrastructure -- gradually collapses the enemy's ability to wage war economically and logistically, rather than through decisive battlefield maneuver.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Defines an alternative theory of victory centered on economic/logistical attrition via long-range strike -- relevant to assessing future Ukrainian strike-capability procurement and its effect on Russian energy/industrial infrastructure risk.
insights.quote: Victory, in this view, comes through economic and logistical collapse rather than decisive battlefield action.

insights.claim: Recent Ukrainian pushes in the south followed the whitelisting of Ukraine-based Starlink terminals, which triggered connection and communication failures on the Russian side -- an example cited of opportunistic, technology-enabled offensive action under the Technologist model.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: A concrete example of commercial satellite-communications infrastructure (Starlink) functioning as a battlefield weapon system -- relevant to how satcom/space-infrastructure companies factor into modern warfare risk and geopolitics.
insights.quote: Offensive operations, rather than serving as the key to victory, become momentary and opportunistic—such as the recent pushes in the south following the whitelisting of Ukraine-based Starlink terminals, which triggered connection and communication failures on the Russian side.

themes.theme: Synthesis: tools must be used together, not as ideology

insights.claim: A senior USF officer told the authors not to reduce the AFU's future to a simple dichotomy between old and new: unmanned systems are 'a single tool in the commander's toolbox,' increasingly essential but still just one capability among many that must be selected carefully alongside others.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: A grounded practitioner view that should temper both bullish drone-only and skeptic legacy-only investment theses in defense tech -- the winning model is combined-arms integration, not single-technology dominance.
insights.quote: Unmanned systems, he explained, are a single tool in the commander's toolbox. Increasingly essential, but still just one capability among many that must be used together and selected carefully to achieve full operational success.

insights.claim: Unmanned systems alone cannot take a heavily fortified position, yet on the 2026 Ukrainian battlefield it is not possible to accomplish that task without them -- heavy artillery and armour are still needed to destroy hardened targets, and infantry is still needed to move in and hold ground once cleared.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: A precise causal claim about complementarity (not substitution) between drones and legacy hardware -- key for modeling future defense procurement mixes and which sectors (drones vs. armor vs. artillery) retain durable demand.
insights.quote: Unmanned systems alone cannot take a heavily fortified position; yet in the Ukrainian battlefield of 2026, it is not possible to accomplish that task without them.

insights.claim: Ukraine's domestic command-and-control system, DELTA, is designed specifically to link the full range of military capabilities together via live feed, matching the most appropriate tool to any given battlefield task rather than privileging one force type.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Names a specific Ukrainian C2 software system (DELTA) whose design philosophy -- tool-agnostic integration -- could be a template or acquisition target for NATO C2 modernization efforts.
insights.quote: This, indeed, is the purpose of Ukraine's domestic C2 system, DELTA: to link the full range of military capabilities together via live feed and to put the most appropriate tool to any given battlefield task.

insights.claim: The authors frame the ultimate unresolved question as whether robotic integration proves that the fundamentals of war have changed (requiring revolutionary restructuring) or that war changes slowly and victory still comes from adherence to fundamentals -- with the AFU's evolving shape serving as the strongest evidence either way.
insights.speaker: Jacob Parakilas
insights.so_what: Frames Ukraine as the live natural experiment for a defining question in modern military doctrine -- outcome will shape global defense procurement priorities (autonomous systems vs. traditional platforms) for a generation.
insights.quote: The question is whether this robotic integration ends up proving that the fundamentals of war have changed... or that war changes slowly and victory comes from paying heed to fundamentals.
